options: One fact table at the center, with dimension tables connected directly to it
Tables chained together in a single long sequence
Every table connected to every other table
A model with only dimension tables and no fact table
questions.explain: Star schema places one fact table at the center, with each dimension table connected directly to it — giving the layout its star-like shape.

questions.q: In Power BI, where can you see the shape of your model's relationships as a diagram?
options: The Filters pane
The Format pane
Model view
Data view
questions.explain: Model view shows every table and the relationship lines connecting them, making the star (or non-star) shape of your model visible.

questions.q: Why does a star schema make filtering more predictable than a looped or chained table layout?
options: Every dimension table has exactly one, direct path to the fact table
It automatically sorts every table alphabetically
It reduces the number of columns in the fact table
Star schema removes the need for any relationships
questions.explain: With one direct route from each dimension to the fact table, there's no ambiguity about which path a filter should travel — unlike a loop, where two paths might reach the same table.

questions.q: Where should a hierarchy like Category → Subcategory → Product be built?
options: From columns within a single dimension table
It can't be built in Power BI
Split evenly across the fact table and a dimension table
Inside the fact table only
questions.explain: A hierarchy needs all its levels in one table to work cleanly. If Category and Product are split into separate tables (a snowflake design), you can't build one hierarchy spanning both.

questions.q: What design keeps a dimension split across multiple related tables instead of one?
options: A factless fact table
A junk dimension
A snowflake
A star schema
questions.explain: A snowflake dimension normalizes a single entity, like Product, across multiple related tables — the opposite of consolidating it into one dimension table.
